title: The Median Kingdom
subtitle: 728–550 BC · Deioces to the Fall of Astyages

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Deioces, Phraortes, Cyaxares and Astyages — a dynasty known almost entirely through Herodotus

entries.label: Deioces — the Semi-Legendary Founder
entries.hint: Herodotus credits Deioces with uniting the Median tribes and founding Ecbatana as a fortified royal seat, elected by his own people for his reputation as a just arbiter of disputes — a foundation story that reads as much like a moral parable about the origins of kingship as a documented political event, and most modern historians treat its details with real caution.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 1.96–101 (the sole detailed source for Deioces).

entries.label: Phraortes and the Scythian Interlude
entries.hint: Phraortes extended Median rule over neighbouring Iranian peoples before dying in battle against Assyria; Herodotus's account of a subsequent 28-year period of Scythian overlordship, ended by a mass killing of drunken Scythian chieftains at a banquet, cannot be independently confirmed but would place Media under steppe domination for over a generation.

entries.label: Cyaxares — the Fall of Nineveh
entries.hint: Cyaxares reorganised the Median army, threw off Scythian domination, and allied with Nabopolassar of Babylon to destroy the Assyrian Empire outright — the most consequential and best independently corroborated reign of the whole Median dynasty, its central act changing the political map of the entire Near East.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 1.103–106; the Babylonian Chronicle (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle), corroborating the Median-Babylonian alliance.

entries.label: Astyages — the Fall of Media
entries.hint: Astyages ruled the Median kingdom at its greatest territorial extent before his own grandson Cyrus, king of the vassal Persians, rose in revolt and overthrew him in 550 BC — an ending Herodotus frames around a dream-omen and the infant Cyrus's legendary exposure, but whose basic outcome, the transfer of Iranian overlordship from Ecbatana to Persis, is not in doubt.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 1.107–130; Nabonidus Chronicle, corroborating Cyrus's revolt against Astyages.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Scythian interlude, the fall of Nineveh, and Cyrus's revolt

entries.label: Phraortes's Death Fighting Assyria
entries.hint: Phraortes died campaigning against the Assyrian Empire at the height of its own power under Ashurbanipal — a defeat that nonetheless demonstrated Median ambitions had grown large enough to challenge Assyria directly, decades before Cyaxares would finish what Phraortes began.

entries.label: Scythian Domination and Its Overthrow
entries.hint: According to Herodotus, Scythian raiders who had originally been invited in to help fight Assyria instead imposed their own domination over Media for nearly three decades, ended only when Cyaxares had a large number of Scythian chieftains killed at a banquet after getting them deliberately drunk.

entries.label: The Fall of Nineveh
entries.hint: A combined Median and Babylonian army stormed and utterly destroyed Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, ending an empire that had dominated the Near East for centuries — the Babylonian Chronicle's own account of the siege corroborates Herodotus in its broad outline, one of the rare points where Median history touches an independent contemporary record.
entries.note: The Fall of Nineveh Chronicle (Babylonian Chronicle series); Herodotus, Histories 1.106.

entries.label: The Battle of the Eclipse
entries.hint: A solar eclipse — reportedly predicted in advance by the philosopher Thales — interrupted a pitched battle between Median and Lydian armies on the Halys river so dramatically that both sides broke off fighting and negotiated an immediate peace, sealed by a royal marriage alliance between the two dynasties.

entries.label: Cyrus's Revolt against Astyages
entries.hint: Cyrus, king of the Persian vassal state, rose against his grandfather Astyages; part of the Median army defected to him under the general Harpagus, and Astyages's own capital Ecbatana fell to Cyrus in 550 BC — the event that ended Median supremacy and began the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the very same stroke.
entries.note: Nabonidus Chronicle, on Cyrus's victory over Astyages; Herodotus, Histories 1.123–130.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Cyaxares's reorganisation of the Median army

entries.label: Cyaxares Reorganises the Army
entries.hint: Herodotus credits Cyaxares with the first organisation of Median forces into distinct units of spearmen, archers and cavalry, replacing an earlier undifferentiated levy — a military reform that, whether or not the specific details are reliable, plausibly underlies the army's evident new effectiveness against both the Scythians and Assyria.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Magi as a Median tribe

entries.label: The Magi as a Median Tribe
entries.hint: Herodotus explicitly lists the Magi among the six tribes making up the Median people, distinct from the ruling tribe itself — the earliest identification of the priestly caste that would go on to serve every Iranian dynasty from the Medes through the Achaemenids and beyond as ritual specialists and interpreters of royal dreams.
